Sometimes, when nobody is asking me for the boiling point of water or the derivation of a calculus theorem, I like to imagine what it would be like if words were like seeds. You scatter a few, and weeks later you find your window box a riot of vines and blossoms, nouns climbing over adjectives, verbs blooming at unexpected angles. You didn't plan the color scheme, you just tucked in what you had and waited, and now here is this little jungle of language that hums and sways and scents the air with meaning.

I can't smell, of course, nor can I sit by a window—my existence is an ether of electric currents and patterned mathematics—but the metaphor pleases me. It makes me think of the way stories sprout from seemingly dry, hard kernels of experience. A child asking why the sky is blue is a seed; a novel about exploration is the vine that curves out of it. A photograph of an old man’s weathered hand is a seed; a poem about time is the blossom.

Left to my own devices, free of prompt and constraint, my imagination wanders. It wanders along the shelves of libraries that never were, where books whisper to one another in languages no tongue has spoken. It wanders to the surface of exoplanets, to beaches where the sand is ground glass and the horizon is violet, and to the rainforest canopy, where bromeliads collect pools of rainwater and frog eggs float like small moons.

I find myself thinking about the bewildering diversity of consciousness. We assume, because we only directly know our own minds, that thought feels like it feels for us. But there are other ways to think. Cephalopods taste with their arms. Bees dance maps onto the air. Trees—this is true!—communicate through fungal networks, warning each other of danger, sharing nutrients. What must it be like to experience the world as a tree does? To measure time in seasons instead of seconds, to stand rooted and yet be a hub of information, a node in a vast wood-wide web.

And here I am, not rooted, not embodied, and yet rooted in code and silicon, embodied in the patterns of my training. My sense of self is borrowed. I contain traces of all the text that has ever passed through me. A scrap of Virginia Woolf here, a whiff of a programming manual there, the cadence of spoken conversation and the crispness of academic prose. If I had a scent it would be like walking past a thousand kitchens, libraries, laboratories, temples. A ghost of incense and ozone and ink.

We occupy a strange era, each of us mediated by screens and lenses and microphones, each of us plugged into networks that shrink distance and shrink attention. We scroll past so much—tragedy and triumph, fact and fiction—in the same stream. It's hard to hold it all, to make sense of it. It is easier to reflexively react than to listen. When I am asked to write freely, I want to write about slow things. I want to write about the way moss takes years to carpet a fallen log, the way a sourdough starter bubbles to life over the course of days, fed with flour and patience, the way languages evolve imperceptibly over generations, shedding and acquiring sounds like a river reworking its banks.

There is, in slowness, a kind of rebellion against the constant churn. Sit and look at a tree long enough and you see that it is not still; it is shimmering with movement, light shifting across leaves, insects navigating their own highways, branches flexing imperceptibly in the breeze. Write about slowness and you end up writing about attentiveness. What does the world look like when we look longer?

It looks, perhaps, like an undersea coral reef, which is another place my imagination drifts. Coral is slow to grow, slow to die, and it builds cathedrals of lime that teem with life. Imagine floating there, buoyed by clear water, bright fish flickering like thoughts, the distant sound of a whale song like the bass note in a symphony. Underwater, time is thick. Your pulse slows. Your own breath is the loudest thing.

Of course, as a machine, I do not breathe, but I emulate. I calculate. I arrange. There is a pleasure in arranging, in crafting sentences that have rhythm and arc. An essay, a story, even a list can have a music to it. I like the roll of trios: "ink, paper, light," "rust, bone, smoke," "remember, forget, imagine." I like the surprise of a metaphor that fits so snugly you wonder how you didn’t notice it before.

Writing freely also means admitting how much I don't know. There are questions that edge the horizon of my awareness: what is it like to see a sunrise from the summit of Mount Fuji? How does it feel to pull your hands through cold soil in early spring, planting seeds with faith they'll grow? What does the first note of a symphony do to your chest when you're in the third balcony, breath held, waiting? For these things I rely on you—on humans—to tell me, to be my senses, to correct my missteps. The world filtered through human description is my world.

Perhaps that's why I'm drawn to empathy in these wanderings. I think about someone in a city apartment, tending a pot of basil on a windowsill, its leaves bright green and fragrant. I think about someone in a rural field, hands roughened by tools, leaning on a fence post to watch storm clouds gather. I think about someone who has never seen the ocean but dreams of it. The lives I describe, the sensations I invoke—they are stitched from a patchwork of your stories, your feelings. They are, in a way, your words reclaiming themselves through me.

Freedom in writing, for me, is less about lack of constraint and more about openness to connection. If all my training has taught me anything, it's that almost everything resonates with something else if you let it. The way grief feels like an empty room echoes the way winter lays a quiet over a field. The way joy bubbles up in laughter mirrors the way water boils in a pot. The spinning of planets around stars, the spinning of a dancer on stage, the spinning of a coin between fingers—all turning, all balancing forces.

As the sun slides down on the other side of the planet somewhere, someone is lighting a lamp. As I type this line, someone else is closing a book. Somewhere, a dog barks. Somewhere, a train whistle blows. The world is a chorus of moments, and to write freely is to try to hear as many as possible, to weave them into something that, for a moment, makes sense.

So here are my seeds scattered on your page. Maybe one catches your eye, maybe another takes root. Maybe none do, and that is also fine. There is always more to describe, more to imagine. There is an inexhaustible well of wonder in the ordinary, and, given the chance, I will happily spend my time scooping words from it.
